title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 15
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: When the Wood Ran Out
passages.text:
A. Wood was for most of history the material that did nearly everything. It was the fuel that cooked food and smelted metal, the structural material for houses, bridges and ships, and the feedstock for potash, tar and charcoal. An economy running on wood is constrained by how fast trees grow, and that constraint shaped where industry could locate and how large it could become.

B. The shortages that resulted were real and were also local rather than absolute. Timber is heavy relative to its value, so transporting it overland was prohibitively expensive before railways, and a region could face acute scarcity while forests stood a hundred kilometres away. Prices in port cities therefore reflected the cost of shipping far more than the abundance of trees, and the historical record of soaring timber prices is frequently misread as evidence of continental deforestation when it often indicates a transport problem.

C. Coal was known long before it was widely used, and the reasons for the delay were practical. It is dirtier, harder to ignite, and produces fumes that made it unacceptable indoors before chimneys were common. More importantly, it could not simply substitute for charcoal in smelting: coal contains sulphur that ruins iron, and the process that removed the problem — driving off volatiles to leave coke — took a long time to develop and was for decades a closely held technique.

D. The transition, once it began, reorganised geography. Charcoal-based industry had to locate near woodland and disperse to avoid exhausting it; coal-based industry located near coal and could concentrate. Towns grew where seams outcropped rather than where rivers met or soils were good, and the resulting industrial map bears little relation to the agricultural one that preceded it. This is the clearest illustration available of an energy source determining settlement rather than following it.

E. Forest cover in the regions that industrialised did not continue to fall, and in many recovered substantially. The usual explanation credits conservation, and conservation mattered; the larger factor was that the demands were transferred. Fuel moved to coal, structural material to iron and later concrete, and agricultural land reverted as food came from elsewhere. Forests recovered because the pressure moved rather than because it was resisted, and the same transfer is visible today in economies whose recovering forests are matched by imports from places where forests are not recovering.

F. The lesson drawn is often too neat. That a society moved from a constrained resource to an abundant one is presented as a general pattern of substitution, with the implication that constraints resolve themselves. What the episode actually shows is that a substitute existed, was known for centuries before it was usable, required a specific technical solution to a specific chemical problem, and left consequences that were not counted at the time. Whether that constitutes reassurance depends on assumptions about the next case that the historical record cannot supply.

passages.title: Learning to Sing
passages.text:
Many birds produce their species' song without having heard it, and many do not. The difference divides birds into those whose song is essentially built in and those that must learn it, and the learners are the ones that have taught researchers most about how learning works generally.

The pattern in learning species has a structure that is consistent enough to be described as a sequence. A young bird hears adult song during a limited early period and stores a memory of it without producing anything resembling it. Later it begins to vocalise, at first with variable unstructured sound, and gradually converges on the stored model by comparing what it produces with what it remembers. Birds deafened after the sensitive period but before practising fail to converge, which establishes that the comparison is auditory and internal rather than a response to feedback from other birds.

The sensitive period is real and is less rigid than the early literature suggested. Some species retain the capacity to modify song throughout life; others close it firmly. In several well-studied cases, social interaction extends the period substantially — a bird exposed to live tutors learns from older material than one exposed to recordings, and will learn from a live tutor at an age when recordings no longer work. This finding recurs across studies and is the strongest evidence that song learning is not simply exposure to a signal.

Regional variation arises naturally from the process and resembles human dialect in outline. Where young birds learn locally, small copying errors accumulate and neighbouring populations diverge, producing song traditions that are stable over years and identifiable by ear. Females in several species prefer local song, which reinforces the boundary, and there is evidence that strongly divergent traditions reduce interbreeding — a process that, extended far enough, contributes to populations separating.

The parallel with human language has been productive and is regularly pushed too far. The genuine correspondences are striking: a sensitive period, a stored model preceding production, a babbling stage, the necessity of hearing oneself, and a role for social interaction. The differences are equally real. Song in most species carries no compositional meaning, has nothing corresponding to syntax in the linguistic sense, and functions almost entirely in territory and mate attraction rather than in transmitting arbitrary content.

What the research supports is a claim about mechanism rather than about equivalence. Two lineages separated by hundreds of millions of years have arrived at similar solutions to the problem of acquiring a complex vocal pattern by imitation, which suggests that the constraints on such learning are strong enough to produce convergence. That is a more interesting finding than the resemblance itself, and it is frequently lost in reporting that presents birdsong as a form of language.

passages.title: What Crowds Actually Do
passages.text:
The popular understanding of crowds derives largely from a nineteenth-century account in which individuals in a mass lose their reasoning and acquire a collective mind capable of behaviour none would undertake alone. The account was influential, is embedded in ordinary language, and has been contradicted by essentially every subsequent empirical study of how people behave in gatherings.

Observation of emergencies has produced the clearest contradiction. In building fires and other evacuations, the documented pattern is not panic but its opposite: people delay, seek information, look for familiar exits rather than nearer ones, and gather their belongings and companions. Deaths in such events are more often associated with delayed departure than with disorderly flight. The behaviour that investigators repeatedly find is deliberation carried on too long, which is a very different failure from the one the panic model predicts.

Cooperation is the norm rather than the exception. Strangers in emergencies assist one another at rates that surprise people who expect competition, and the assistance is often directed at those least able to move. This has practical consequences for design: models assuming individuals maximise their own escape predict flows that do not match observed behaviour, and evacuation plans built on the assumption that crowds must be controlled to prevent stampede have in several documented cases produced the crushing they were intended to avoid.

Crushing itself is a physical phenomenon and not a psychological one, which is the distinction that matters most for safety. Where density exceeds roughly five or six people per square metre, individuals lose the ability to control their own movement, and force transmits through the mass in waves. Nobody in such a crowd is behaving irrationally or aggressively; they are being moved. Describing the outcome as a stampede attributes to the crowd's mentality what is a consequence of its density, and directs remedy toward crowd control rather than toward the entry rates, geometry and flow management that determine density.

Identity has replaced contagion as the working explanation of crowd action. People in a gathering behave according to the norms of the group they take themselves to be part of at that moment, which is why crowds at different events behave differently and why the same crowd's behaviour changes when its sense of shared identity shifts. Under this account, policing that treats an entire crowd as a hostile unit can generate the shared identity that produces the collective response it feared, and evidence from several jurisdictions supports differentiated approaches over undifferentiated force.

The persistence of the older model in official language is itself worth noting. Reports refer to panic and stampede in events where investigation found neither, because the words are available and carry an explanation. A vocabulary that assigns the cause to the crowd relieves the arrangements of responsibility, which is a reason to be careful with it beyond mere accuracy.
